document.title: IIR [Excised]/Veteran Afghanistan Traveler's Analysis of Al Qaeda and Taliban Exploitable Weaknesses
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
document.note: [Secret] DIA report on the status of the Taliban and al-Qaeda and strategy for the coming US-led war, stressing human intelligence. Notes that Bin Laden's al-Qaeda network expanded under the safe sanctuary extended by the Taliban following Pakistan directives, elucidating the ISI connection.

sources_cited: DIA Intelligence Information Report (IIR) dated 24 Sep 2001 from a veteran Afghanistan traveler
key_claims: Eventually the Taliban and al Qaeda will war with each other; al Qaeda has failed to integrate with Afghans or the Taliban and could consume its host.
Al Qaeda's key weakness is its elite self-perception and the 'power of names', which can be exploited psychologically.
Bin Laden's network expanded under Taliban sanctuary extended following Pakistani directives.
The Zhawar camp was built by ISI-funded Pakistani contractors under Jalaluddin Haqqani's patronage, and the real host was the ISI, raising questions about the ISI-bin Laden relationship.
The Taliban's mobile deployment, lacking local identity, created cracks with ordinary Afghans, as shown by the February 2000 Khost uprising.
Jalaluddin Haqqani was rumored to be increasingly unhappy with the Taliban, and al Qaeda may treat parts of Paktia as its own.
Pashtun tribal uprisings around Khost and in Nimruz signal cracks between the Taliban and ordinary Afghans.
Al-Qaeda is non-indigenous and lacks local popular support, making its Afghan hosts prone to resentment.
Eventual Taliban–al-Qaeda conflict is expected as al-Qaeda grows strong enough to consume its host.
Recommended approach is stand-off air strikes away from cities, plus limited SF ground deployment within opposition territory rather than mass ground forces.
Strikes should target al-Qaeda and the 055 Brigade while sparing Taliban aircraft to emphasize the distinction between them.
Some Stinger missiles are assumed to be held by al-Qaeda near Osama bin Laden, with the rest stockpiled near cities and airports.
Long-term goal is moderating or removing the Taliban and creating a coalition government free of Pakistani interference.
